A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same efficiency-aware code-generation study despite renaming. Their text, tables, figures and equations support comparison. v3 ends with references; v4 additionally contains Appendix A.

before.justification: v3 reports original fine-tuning experiments across code-generation benchmarks in Tables 2–7 and an empirical training-data efficiency study in Figure 3.

after.justification: v4 retains those experiments and adds original platform comparisons, baseline evaluations, ENAMEL results, repeated-execution measurements and a case study in its appendix.

M1.justification: Both versions use multiple LLMs to generate candidates, select efficient solutions through execution profiling, and perform supervised fine-tuning. SWIFTCODER becomes EFFICODER, with its dataset named EFFIINSTRUCT. Appendix A.4 details test augmentation already indicated in v3, without establishing a changed procedure.

E1.justification: v4 adds ENAMEL evaluation in A.7 and tests generated code across seven Python-version/CPU environments in A.3/Table 8. These extend evaluation coverage within code generation; Table 1 retains the same training sources and five languages, and the existing benchmark tasks remain.

E2.justification: v3 compares against PIE and Mercury in Table 7. v4 retains these, identifies the existing PIE strategy as All, and adds comparisons with PIE HQ, All w/Perf-Cond, HQ + Self-Play, and EffiLearner in Tables 9–10. This substantially broadens the evaluated alternatives.

E3.justification: The original training hyperparameters and reported greedy-decoding setting remain unchanged. Added evaluation designs include seven software/hardware combinations, ENAMEL eff@k and pass@k at k = 1, 10 and 100, and an EffiLearner comparison restricted to tasks addressed by all compared models.

E4.justification: v4 adds a training/evaluation overlap check in footnote 2, environment robustness tests in A.3, execution-variability analysis in A.10, and an actual generated-code case study in A.9/Figure 5. These address contamination, measurement stability and optimization behavior beyond v3's retained preliminary analyses.

E5.justification: Unlike v3, A.10/Table 12 reports five executions of fine-tuned Qwen2.5-Coder-7B with means and standard deviations. These are execution repeats, not training-seed replications. Exact variability is inconsistently documented: A.3 reports an ET standard deviation of 0.00548 seconds, whereas A.10/Table 12 reports 0.00.

E6.justification: Existing numerical rows in Tables 1–7 are unchanged, but Table 7 adds original-model controls. Tables 8–12 and Figure 5 introduce substantial new results. For example, Table 11 reports ENAMEL baseline/fine-tuned Qwen eff@1 values of 0.373/0.458 and pass@1 values of 0.589/0.739; these are newly reported comparisons, not revised v3 scores.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 supplies formulas and explanations for ET, NET, MU, NMU, TMU and NTMU, all already used in v3. This documents existing metric calculations rather than introducing new theory or substantive mathematical reasoning. Neither version contains theoretical proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central contributions: a versatile dataset-construction framework, an efficiency-oriented instruction dataset, and improved correctness and efficiency through fine-tuning. The headline results remain identical. Distinguishing EFFICODER from EFFIINSTRUCT clarifies naming without changing these scientific claims.

C2.justification: Section 4.4 adds explanations attributing performance to multilingual coverage, efficiency filtering and dataset scale. A.3 discusses environment dependence, while A.9 attributes the case-study speedup to pruning redundant recursion. These substantially expand interpretation, although the proposed contributing factors are not isolated through ablations.

D1.justification: v4 adds a code/data availability statement with a repository address, a completion prompt in A.1, metric-calculation details in A.2, and GPT-3.5-turbo test generation and reference-solution filtering details in A.4. Table 8 names software/hardware configurations. These materially improve documentation; unchanged training settings do not establish reruns.

R1.justification: v4 adds Liu et al. (2024b) and Sun et al. (2024), removes Anil et al. (2023), and expands positioning against PIE and Mercury around automation, language coverage and scale in A.8. The broader related-work organization and novelty positioning remain.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section sequence largely remain, with terminology changes, light rewriting, an Impact Statement heading, acknowledgments and appendix organization. Editing also introduces missing dataset names in several results paragraphs, while the appendix retains legacy Effi-Code names and rebuttal-style references.

P2.justification: v4 adds five result tables, a substantial code-comparison figure and a boxed prompt. Table 7 gains control rows, Table 1 moves above Figure 4, and existing captions and labels are revised. This materially expands the visual presentation while retaining the original figures and results displays.

improvement.justification: v4 strengthens empirical support through platform robustness tests and broader comparisons, and improves reproducibility through explicit prompting, test-generation details and a code/data access pointer. These address omissions in v3. The gains are limited by new reporting defects: Table 10's memory-reduction percentages contradict its values, runtime standard deviations conflict between A.3 and Table 12, and missing names impair the main prose. The established core results remain intact.
